title: Shared Database Anti-Pattern
description: Understand why sharing a database between microservices is an anti-pattern and how to avoid it.

data.text: Sharing a database between multiple microservices is one of the most common anti-patterns in microservices architecture. Amazon and Netflix both fell into this trap early on and suffered from tight coupling, schema conflicts, and cascading failures.
What Is the Shared Database Anti-Pattern?

The shared database anti-pattern occurs when multiple microservices connect to the same database or schema. Services inadvertently become coupled through the data model, and any schema change requires coordinating across teams.

data.title: Consequences of Shared Databases
items: Tight coupling: Schema changes require cross-team coordination
Technology lock-in: All services must use the same database
Single point of failure: Database downtime affects all services
Performance contention: One heavy query can slow down all services
Security risks: Hard to enforce data access boundaries

data.title: The Distributed Monolith
data.text: A shared database turns microservices into a distributed monolith. You get the overhead of distributed systems without the autonomy benefits.

data.title: Example: Shared Database Scenario
data.code:
-- Shared database with multiple services
-- users table (owned by User Service)
-- orders table (owned by Order Service)

-- Problem: Order Service needs user email for notifications
-- Bad solution: Order Service queries users table directly
-- This creates a hidden dependency

-- Better: Order Service calls User Service API
-- User Service exposes: GET /users/{id}
-- Order Service gets email through API, not SQL

items.question: Is sharing a database ever acceptable?
items.answer: Only as a temporary measure during migration from a monolith. Plan to extract services with their own databases as soon as possible.

items.question: What if my team is small?
items.answer: Even small teams benefit from database per service. It reduces coupling and allows independent evolution. Use Docker Compose for local development.

items.question: How do I migrate from a shared database?
items.answer: Use the Strangler Fig pattern. Extract one service at a time, starting with the least coupled. Use change data capture (CDC) to keep data synchronized during migration.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Shared databases create tight coupling between services
Any schema change requires cross-team coordination
Database per service is the recommended approach
data.takeaway: Avoid shared databases; they turn microservices into a distributed monolith.
